edition: Issue #014 - A 12th-placed shield holder, a $4b sleeper-train dream, and Sam’s jam
tagline: Your 3-minute break. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: A 12th-placed team holds the Ranfurly Shield all summer - rugby’s prize that ignores the league table
stories.summary: Counties Manukau, who finished 12th out of 14 this NPC season, beat Hawke’s Bay 12-7 in Pukekohe to keep the Ranfurly Shield over the summer.

body.text: Counties Manukau have kept the Ranfurly Shield, repelling Hawke’s Bay 12-7 at Navigation Homes Stadium in Pukekohe. They led 12-0 at halftime on tries from back-rower Adam Brash and Melani Matavao, before the Magpies dominated the second half and Darby Lancaster crossed for their only try. Counties captain Jimmy Tupou went off injured in the 53rd minute but his side hung on. The win caps a late-season resurgence after Counties claimed the shield from Northland last weekend - and it means the trophy stays in Pukekohe over the summer. The kicker: Counties finished the season in 12th place out of 14 teams and missed the playoffs entirely.

The Ranfurly Shield is rugby’s most beautiful, most stubborn idea: it does not care about your league table, it only cares who actually beats the person holding it. So a team that finished 12th out of 14, that will watch the playoffs from the couch, gets to spend an entire summer being the guard dog of the hardest-to-win prize in the sport. That is the rugby equivalent of clearing the garden all summer while the neighbours argue about the letterbox. Counties took the shield off Northland last weekend and just defended it against Hawke’s Bay this weekend, and somewhere a future history of New Zealand rugby is writing itself about the team that finished 12th and still held the crown. Sport, we love you when you do this.

RNZ (3 Oct 2026): Counties Manukau beat Hawke’s Bay 12-7 at Navigation Homes Stadium, Pukekohe to retain the Ranfurly Shield. Counties led 12-0 at halftime after tries from back-rower Adam Brash and Melani Matavao; Hawke’s Bay scored when Darby Lancaster crossed after a dummy pass from halfback Folau Fakatava (Harry Godfrey with the conversion). Counties captain Jimmy Tupou went off injured in the 53rd minute. Counties claimed the shield from Northland the previous weekend and finished the NPC season in 12th place out of 14 with four wins, missing the playoffs; Hawke’s Bay finished fifth and miss hosting a quarterfinal.

stories.headline: The $4b question: Greens dream of sleeper trains while the other leaders argue about a white elephant
stories.summary: The Green Party’s election plan would run an Auckland-Wellington overnight service, Christchurch-Dunedin passenger rail and extend Te Huia to Tauranga, at a cost of about $4 billion - drawing the white-elephant line from National.

body.text: The Green Party has unveiled a roughly four-billion-dollar passenger-rail plan for the election: an overnight Auckland-Wellington sleeper service, passenger rail between Christchurch and Dunedin, and an extension of the Te Huia Hamilton-Auckland route to Tauranga. Transport spokesperson Julie Anne Genter makes the case that the tracks already exist, so they should be used. The response from the other leaders was swift and familiar. NZ First leader and coalition Rail Minister Winston Peters says the idea has been around for over 100 years and the job is to make it work; National leader Christopher Luxon says he will not back taxpayer money going into a white elephant and remains committed to his roads of national significance.

Every election cycle, someone dusts off the sleeper train, and every election cycle the country has the same conversation at slightly higher volumes. The Greens say the tracks are already sitting there, unused. Peters says the idea is a century old and makes a principled stand of not ruling anything out, right before mentioning a thousand announcements and a business case the Greens would apparently not recognise if it hit them. Luxon says he needs seventeen roads and his apology is already drafted. Somewhere underneath all that spray is a fairly sober thought: a country that might genuinely enjoy naps between its two biggest cities is watching four billion dollars get passed around a room like a takeaway box nobody actually wants to open. The tracks are there. The argument is not about whether trains work, it is about who gets to spend the money and call it theirs.

RNZ (3 Oct 2026): The Green Party announced, if elected, an overnight Auckland-Wellington rail service, passenger rail between Christchurch and Dunedin, and an extension of the Te Huia route to Tauranga. Transport spokesperson Julie Anne Genter said the tracks already exist. NZ Herald (3 Oct 2026) put the total cost at about $4.02 billion ($2.57b initial services - a $110m Auckland-Wellington pilot, $2.05b Auckland-Tauranga, $410m Christchurch-Dunedin - plus $1.45b Stage Two). NZ First leader Winston Peters (coalition Rail Minister) said the idea has been around for over 100 years and his job is to make sure it is viable; National leader Christopher Luxon said he will not back taxpayer funding of a white elephant that is not commercially viable, preferring National’s 17 roads of national significance.

stories.headline: Sam Neill’s real legacy is apricot jam, a famous pig, and the tuis that came back
stories.summary: Two months after losing Sir Sam Neill, spring has sprung on the vines at Two Paddocks; the apricots took a frost hit but the pig’s Instagram status and the native plantings carry the legacy on.

body.text: It has been a little over two months since we lost Sir Sam Neill, and at Two Paddocks Winery in Central Otago spring has sprung on the vines ahead of the 2027 vintage. General manager Jacqui Murphy told RNZ’s Saturday Morning the farm lost most of this season’s apricot crop to frost - about 80 percent of four trees, which she called no national disaster but enough to leave everyone a bit miffed, because Sam used those apricots to make the jam he loved. The pigs are thriving, the native plantings Sam put in have brought the tuis and bellbirds back, and there are plans to open Red Bank Farm and Vineyard for tours from December.

Hollywood gets the front pages, but the softest truth about one of the world’s best-known actors is that the whole planet’s most-shared part of him might be a pig. Sam Neill’s Instagram was famously, gloriously pig-filled, and his genuine hobby was making apricot jam on a farm in Central Otago and hanging up art bought from local young artists. No nasty sprays, a couple of very loved rescue pigs, a few thousand native trees that brought the songbirds back - that is the legacy you pour into a glass and, from December, might actually be able to wander around and see for yourself. The famous blockbuster roles got him the name; the quiet farm is why the name is going to be fondly remembered for a very long time. Some people spend a fortune to look like they live a rustic life. Sam Neill just did it, jam and all.

RNZ Life / Saturday Morning (3 Oct 2026; story by Dan Satherley): About two months after Sir Sam Neill died at 78, Two Paddocks Winery in Central Otago is heading into the 2027 vintage. General manager Jacqui Murphy told RNZ’s Saturday Morning that about 80 percent of the season’s apricot crop (roughly four trees, no frost protection) was lost, with some of Neill’s Sam jam still in the cupboard. Production is kept as organic as possible. Two Paddocks’ Instagram confirmed pigs Brian and Amy are thriving. Neill’s native plantings around the farm brought back tuis, bellbirds and songbirds. Tours of Red Bank Farm and Vineyard are planned from December.
